contentSummary: The Earth's primary movements are Rotation (spinning on its axis) from West to East once in every 24 hours causing day and night and Revolution (orbiting around the Sun) once in 365¼ days causing seasons. These movements significantly impact life on Earth by causing day and night cycles, seasons, and variations in the amount of sunlight different regions receive, influencing climate and weather patterns. a. o The Earth moves in space in two distinct ways namely Rotation and Revolution o Rotation is the spinning of the Earth on its tilted axis. o The Earth rotates from West to East once in every 24 hours. o The effects of rotation of the Earth results in day and night, difference in time at different lines of longitude, deflection of winds and ocean currents, revolution of the moon around the earth and tidal changes. o Revolution refers to Earth's orbital motion around the Sun every 365¼ days. o The effects of revolution of the Earth includes; changes in the length of day and night from day to day, changes in the altitude of the midday sun and changes in seasons. o The combined effect of Earth's revolution, rotation, and axial tilt produce seasonal variations in the North and South Hemispheres. o In general, they influence the global climate, wind and ocean current patterns, and the Sun's heat distribution. e. Earth’s rotations affect time and daily activities. o It causes day and night, influencing work schedules, travel and business hours o It creates time zones affecting global communication and event planning Earths revolution determines seasons o Affects farming o Influences tourism and outdoor events c. Learning and Teaching Materials o Weather instruments such as thermometers and wind vanes o Model of the Earth to demonstrate planetary movements in the Solar system. o Weather maps, diagrams depicting the Earth’s surface o Calendars to plan and track events o Video showing rotation and revolution of the Earth d.

contentSummary: The Globe comprises of a number of imaginary lines that crisscross it. These lines constitute of what is called the Earth’s graticule. It is composed of two main sets of lines namely latitudes and longitudes. These lines are used to precisely measure and locate positions on the Earth’s surface. a. o The Earth’s graticule is the network of lines and coordinates that crisscross the globe, providing a framework for mapping, navigation and geographic reference. o Latitude is the angular distance of a point on the earth’s surface, measured in degrees from the centre of the earth. o Lines of latitudes are imaginary lines that run east-west around the Earth, parallel to the equator, hence also called parallel of latitudes. o Important latitudes; the Arctic Circle (66½°), the tropic of Cancer (23½° N), the Equator (0°), the Tropic of Capricorn (23½°) and the Antarctic Circle (66½°). o On the globe they appear as circles becoming smaller pole wards, making the equator the longest parallel and are drawn at 1° interval. o Longitude is the angular distance measured in degrees along the equator east or west of the Greenwich Meridian (0°). o They are lines that run from North Pole to the South Pole, measuring distance east or west of the Prime Meridian (which passes through Greenwich, England). o Longitudes are also known as Meridians. The Greenwich Meridian/Prime Meridian (0°) passes near London and all Meridians radiates from it, East wards or West wards up to 180°. o Longitudes are used in determining local time in relation to the Greenwich Meridian Time (GMT). e. International Date Line involves the following: o The International Date Line is an imaginary line on the Earth’s surface that runs North to South through the middle of the Pacific Ocean following 180 degrees Meridian. o It separates two consecutive calendar days with locations to the West of the line being one day ahead of the locations to the East. o It is not a straight line but zigzagging and deviates from 180 degrees meridian in several places to avoid dividing some islands o When crossing the date line from East to West one loses a day (because of the loss in time one has made) and by crossing the date line from West to East a day is gained (because of the gain encountered in time) o It is a line of longitude where the date changes by exactly one day when it is crossed o When travelling eastwards from Greenwich, time is gained by 24 hours until one reaches the Meridian 180° E and is ahead of GMT. o Similarly, when going westwards from Greenwich, time is lost by 24 hours when one reaches 180°W and is behind GMT c. o Places on the Earth’s surface can be located using imaginary lines (Latitudes and longitudes) o Latitudes runs from west to east, parallel to the equator o Longitudes runs north and south passing through the poles o The intersection of the two set of lines (latitudes and longitudes) pin-point and indicate precise location of a place on the Globe. c. o GIS is a computer-based system that integrate geographic data with spatial analysis and visualization. o It is used in locating places by pinpointing specific locations using geographic coordinates such as latitudes and longitude c. o Latitudes and longitudes are used to locate places, calculation of time and distance. o GPS can be used in planning for route use, search for location when in a new place o Time zoning such as planning for different activities such as conferences, calls, meetings, travel o Generate and read maps. o GPS could be used in tracking of cars, animals in a national parks, theft cases. c. o Standard time is where each country adopts the local time of its Central Meridian e. g Zambia adopted the 30°E longitude as its Central Meridian. o Time Zones are divisions into which the World is divided, that is, 24 belts, each 15° of longitude wide. o Longitudes are used to calculate local time of places in relation to the Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) or World Time. o If the GMT is known, local time can easily be found by either adding or subtracting the difference in the number of hours from the given longitudes. o Therefore, to the East; Gain = Add (E.G.A) and to the West; Lose = Subtract (W.L.S). o The Earth makes one complete rotation of 360° in one day or 24 hours; hence it passes through 15° in every 1 hour. o Since the Earth passes through 15° in every 1 hour, this means it passes through 1° every 4 minutes. o Time is gained (added) by 1 hour as one move eastwards while west wards, time is lost (retarded) by 1 hour as one moves from the GMT respectively. d. Learning and Teaching Materials o Globe and time zone maps to display different longitudes o Compass to show directions of towns o Posters/charts displaying different standard time zones. e. Assessment i.Ask questions to check understanding of: o Time calculation for local times such as Lusaka. o GMT in relation to local time and its significance in calculation of local and standard times o Observe learners calculate local times of different towns using longitudes. o Ask learners to write on why different cities or towns have different times. o Calculating longitudes involve determining the difference between local time and Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). o Determine the local time and GMT of a respective location o Find the difference in time between local time and GMT o Convert time difference to longitude by using the formula: Longitude =Time Difference × 15o c. o Time zones are regions on Earth that follow a uniform standard time at a specific meridian. o Time zones facilitate efficient communication, transportation and economic transactions across the Globe. o Time zones are integrated in the development of technological advancements especially modern technologies such as , GPS systems and computer networks which rely on precise time keeping and coordination. o They are vital in Scientific Research, Navigation and mapping as they provide a common reference point for collecting and analysing data c. o The Erath is a sphere with 360° of latitude of latitude 180° N/S from the Equator o One degree of latitude = 111km (varies slightly due to the Earth’s shape but is generally accurate for basic calculations) o The formula for calculating: Distance = (Difference in Latitude) ×111km o Calculate the distance from Cairo (30° N) to the equator (0°). 30 x 111 Km = 3 330 Km from the equator. o Latitudes are further used to calculate distances places on different hemispheres. Places on different hemispheres Calculate the distance between Zambia (30o S) and Morocco (20o N) Solution o First locate the places involved o Latitude of Zambia = 30o S o Latitude of Morocco = 20o N o Latitude Difference; from South to North = Addition o Thus latitude difference 20o S + 30o N = 50o o Since 1o = 111km o Hence, 500 = (111 x 50) km = 5550km; the distance between Zambia and Morocco o Pilots, Sailors and hikers use latitudes to estimate distance and navigate. o In Geography latitude is important in understanding geographic features such as climate zones and time zones. Places on same hemispheres Calculate the distance between Abuja 10o N and Tripoli 40o N o Locate two places involved o Latitude of Abuja = 10o N o Latitude of Tripoli = 40o N o From North to North = Subtraction o Latitude difference = 400 N – 10o N = 30o o Since 1o = 111km o Then 30o = (111 x 30) km = 3330km o Hence, the distance between Abuja and Tripoli is 3330km d. o Latitude is used to measure the distance North or South of the equator ranging from 0° to 90°. o Learners are encouraged to create a map of local area labelling important landmarks and their latitudes c. o The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal plane and a line of sight to an object above the horizon. o Angle of elevation is based on the position of the midday sun and position of the place. o The angle of elevation can be calculated using the following procedure on the midday sun, when the overhead sun and the place are in the same hemisphere,

contentSummary: 2.8.1. Introduction The Earth’s atmosphere is a mixture of gasses that surrounds the earth. It helps make life possible by providing air, shielding from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation coming from the sun, trapping heat to warm the planet and preventing extreme temperature differences between day and night. The Earth’s atmosphere has five major and several secondary layers that comprise of the Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere and Exosphere. The Atmosphere is a mixture of nitrogen (78%), Oxygen (21%) and other gasses (1%) that surrounds the Earth. These gases combine to absorb ultraviolet radiation from the sun and warm the planet’s surface through the retention. Oxygen is the most important of all the gases in the atmosphere as it support human and animal life. o The first layer of the Earth’s atmosphere is the Troposphere that extends from the surface to between 7km at the poles and 17 km at the equator. o The Troposphere is the lowest layer with decreasing temperature with height. It is the layer we live in and where weather happens. o The second layer is the Stratosphere found between 12km to 50km above. The temperature in this layer increases with height. o The stratosphere houses the ozone layer which absorbs the ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun. This stratospheric ozone provides an important service to life on Earth as it absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. o Ultraviolet rays are harmful heat rays which when exposed to the body can cause skin disease and cancer. o The Mesosphere is the third layer and is above the stratosphere lying between 50km and 80km. o The Thermosphere is the next layer after the Mesosphere which lies 80km and above. The layer has increased temperature because it is directly heated by the sun. o The Ionosphere is an electrically charged layer which is used for communication and navigation purposes making transmission of Radio short waves possible o The Exosphere is the layer without gases and is mainly used in modern artificial satellite launch. d. o The atmosphere provides essential elements that support life on Earth such as gases, water vapour... o The atmosphere regulates temperature and protects people from harmful radiation. o Climate regulate the influences of weather patterns, climate and global temperatures on the environment. o Human activities such as pollution, cutting down of tree for fuel can affect atmospheric health. o Conservation and protection of the environment requires collective action with the community to come up with conservation measures. c. Learning and Teaching Materials o Posters and charts d. Assessment o Observe learners as they give reports on how they shared information with family and community

e. Summary
Earth's Position in the Solar System
o Earth is the third planet from the Sun in our solar system. It is situated between Venus
and Mars.
o Seasons: Earth's tilt and orbit around the Sun cause the seasons. For example, when the
Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it experiences summer, while the
Southern Hemisphere has winter.
o Solar Energy: Solar panels capture energy from the Sun, which powers homes and
devices. The Sun's position in the solar system makes it a crucial energy source for
Earth.
Shape of the Earth
o Air Travel: The oblate spheroid shape affects flight paths. Pilots use the curvature of
the Earth to plan the most efficient routes, known as great circle routes.
o Satellite Orbits: Satellites orbit around Earth, taking into account its shape to maintain
accurate positioning for GPS, weather forecasting, and communication.
Size of the Earth
o Geography: Knowing Earth's size helps in mapping and navigation. For instance,
understanding the Earth's circumference is essential for global shipping routes and air
travel.
o Climate Zones: The size and shape of Earth create various climate zones, from tropical
regions near the equator to polar regions at the poles.
Graticule of the Earth
o Navigation: Latitude and longitude are used in GPS systems to provide precise
locations. For example, when you use a navigation app to find directions, it relies on
the graticule.
o Time Zones: Longitude lines determine time zones. When you travel across different
longitudes, you adjust your watch to match the local time.
Atmosphere of the Earth
o Weather: The layers of the atmosphere affect weather patterns. For instance, the
troposphere is where most weather events occur, like rain, snow, and storms.
o Breathing Air: The atmosphere's composition is crucial for life. The oxygen we breathe
is part of the atmosphere, and changes in its composition can impact health and the
environment.

contentSummary: 2.5.1. Introduction Weather changes from time to time. Climate is more stable and involves average atmospheric conditions of a large area over a long period of time for example 30 years. In order to understand weather and climate, one needs to observe and interpret daily atmospheric conditions such as temperature, rainfall, wind and humidity. The sub-topic will focus on how learners will use knowledge of weather and climate, elements and factors influencing weather and climate in real-life experiences o Weather refers to the state of the atmosphere at a particular time and place. It is a short term process and can change at any time and affects daily activities. o Climate is the average weather conditions of a place over a long period of time. It is long term, consistent over time, affects ecosystems o When we say it is hot, cloudy or windy we are referring to weather and not climate. o These patterns of weather are recorded for many years to come up with climate of the region. o When we say hot summers or cold winters we are referring to climate d. Elements of Weather and Climate o Temperature: Measure how hot or cold the atmosphere is. Temperature is measured by an instrument called Thermometer. o Rainfall: Water falling from the atmosphere in form showers, hailstones (ice rain) heavy rainfall. It is measured by an instrument called Rain gauge. o Wind speed and direction: Wind is air in motion that has speed and direction. It moves from a place of high pressure to a place of low pressure. Wind speed is measured by an instrument called Cup Anemometer while wind direction is measured by a Wind vane. o Humidity: The amount of water vapour in the air (low humidity is when there is less water vapour in atmosphere, high humidity is when there is more water vapour in the atmosphere and saturated air when air cannot hold any more water vapour. It is measured by an instrument called Hygrometer. o Cloud cover: The amount and type of cloud present in the sky. It is measured by mare observation. o Sunshine: The intensity and duration of sunlight received. It is measured by an instrument called Sunshine Recorder. o Atmospheric air pressure: The weight of air exerted on the earth’s surface. It is measured by an instrument called Barometer. c. o Latitudes; areas near the equator are warmer than those farther away o Altitude; temperatures reduces as one ascends (The higher you go the cooler it becomes). o Water bodies such as lakes and oceans make places cooler or warmer, depending on the season. o Vegetation; forest areas cooler than open areas o Areas near the sea are cooler than those in the interior. o Winds and ocean currents move heat and moist around the globe. o Our environment influences the weather and human activities can also change local climates o Weather and climate affects everyone farmers, pilots fishermen, sports players rely on weather forecasts c. Vegetation o Zambia has Savanna type of vegetation characterized by tall grasses and scattered trees. o This type of climatic region influences vegetation characteristics and human activities. Seasons o Zambia has a tropical climate with three distinct seasons namely cold season, hot season and rainy season. Regional climate variation o The South western part of the country is drier and hotter, the Eastern region is cooler and wetter and lastly the Northern region is warmer and more humid. Winds o Zambia experiences trade winds from the southeast which bring warm, moist air from the Indian Ocean while westerly winds bring warm dry air from the Atlantic Ocean. o During winter, the country experiences easterly winds which bring cool, dry air from the Indian Ocean. Air masses o Zambia is influenced by the tropical air mass which is characterized by high temperatures and high humidity o During winter months the country is influenced by cool South African air mass with low humidity while in summer the country is influenced by the warm moist Congo air mass with high humidity. c. o Check weather forecasts before engaging in outdoor activities o Encourage learners to dress appropriately for weather, including wearing sun glasses, hats rain coats and warm clothes o Learners to stay hydrated during outdoor activities o Plan for outdoor games on days with favourable weather. (Not too cold, hot or rainy). o Learners to plant and maintain garden/field by incorporating knowledge of weather and climate. o School tours should take into account weather and climate c.

contentSummary: 2.4.1. Introduction: Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperatures and weather patterns. Such shifts can be natural, due to changes in the sun's activity or large volcanic eruptions or can be due to human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. The topic is about identifying the causes of climate change and assessing the impact of climate change on human activities. It will also look at disseminating the information on climate change to family and community members for the sake of awareness. Climate change is as a result of natural and human forces impacting on the environment. Human causes of climate change include: o Burning of fossil fuels such as oil, gas, and coal. o Deforestation o Agriculture activities o Pollution Natural causes of climate change include: o El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) effects o Solar irradiance o Volcanic eruptions o Plate tectonics and continental drift d. Climate change has got serious impacts on the environment, human health, the economy and social dynamics. Environmental impacts o Rising temperatures; the Earths average temperature has increased leading to more heatwaves. o Extreme weather events leading to increased frequency of heat waves, drought and heavy rainfall o Loss of biodiversity due to changes in temperature and precipitation patterns leading to loss of plant and animal life Human impacts o Respiratory problems due to changes in air quality Economic impacts o Damage to infrastructure – floods can damage roads, bridges and buildings o Agricultural decline; unpredictable rainfall and drought reduce crop yields especially for maize Zambia’s staple food o Loss of livestock due to temperature and precipitation changes o Energy crisis; Hydro- electric power plants depend on water levels which are affected by droughts leading to power shortages o Loss of livelihoods; farmers, fishermen, and people who rely on natural res struggle as climate conditions change Social impacts o Displacement of people due to natural disasters such as floods and droughts o Vector borne diseases due to changes in temperature and precipitation patterns that support the habitats of disease carrying insects like mosquitoes o Mental health impacts due to temperature changes leading to increased stress, anxiety and trauma. o Heat related illness such as heat exhaustion and heat stroke o Conflicts of resources such as scarce water and arable land can lead to conflicts between communities o Food security due to less food production leads to hunger and malnutrition especially in rural areas c. o Family discussions about climate change are a critical factor influencing communities’ perceptions and behaviors. o Encourage learners to discuss climate change impacts with family members, sharing their knowledge, experiences and concerns o Engage learners and family members in joint projects such as creating a climate resilient gardens or reduce energy consumption. o Invite learners to share personal stories or family experiences related to climate change. o Learners to participate in community events involving climate change affairs. o Appoint learners to be climate change ambassadors to share knowledge and promote climate action within their communities. c.

contentSummary: 2.4.2. Introduction The topic focuses on efforts aimed at coming up with actions and strategies that can reduce or prevent long-term climate change risks. The goal of mitigation is to address the root causes of climate change thereby reducing the severity of climate-related risks such as extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and biodiversity loss. As climate change intensifies, communities around the world face increasing risks from extreme weather events, rising temperatures, and shifting environmental patterns. From hurricanes and wildfires to droughts and floods, these climate-related disasters threaten lives, infrastructure, and livelihoods. The topic focuses on efforts aimed at coming up with actions and strategies that can reduce or prevent long-term climate change risks. To build resilience, individuals and communities must adapt their lifestyles to local climate risks, ensuring they can withstand and recover from environmental hazards more effectively. Adaptation strategies include designing climate-resilient homes, adopting sustainable agricultural practices, modifying daily routines, and leveraging technology for early warnings and disaster preparedness. By understanding local climate vulnerabilities and integrating risk- reducing measures into everyday life, people can safeguard their health, homes, and economies while contributing to broader climate resilience efforts. This topic therefore explores practical approaches to adapting lifestyles to local climate risks, emphasizing proactive solutions that enhance preparedness, reduce vulnerability, and foster sustainable living in an increasingly unpredictable world. Zambia is taking steps to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions and mitigate the effects of climate change. For instance: o Solar Energy: Encourage the use of solar lamps and chargers, which are becoming more accessible in Zambia. It's a great way to harness renewable energy and reduce reliance on non-renewable sources. o Tree Planting: Join or start a tree-planting initiative. Zambia is known for its Miombo woodlands, and planting indigenous trees can help preserve the environment. o Climate Clubs: Participate in school or community climate clubs that focus on local issues and solutions, such as managing waste or conserving water. o Sustainable Transportation: Encourage walking or biking to school if it's safe and feasible. This not only reduces carbon emissions but also promotes physical health. Learners can also be encouraged to use local buses or shared taxis to reduce the number of individual cars on the road. o Local Foods: Support local farmers by choosing fruits and vegetables that are in season. This reduces the carbon footprint associated with transporting goods. o Reduce Plastic Use: Use alternatives to plastic, such as cloth bags for shopping and reusable containers for food and drinks. o Education and Advocacy: Work with local organizations to spread awareness about climate change and sustainability practices. This can be done through community meetings, social media, and local events. o Gardening Projects: Start or join community gardens where families can grow their own vegetables. This promotes local food production and reduces dependence on imported goods. o Upcycling Workshops: Hold workshops to teach others how to repurpose old items into new, useful products. This can include turning plastic bottles into planters or old clothes into reusable shopping bags. o Renewable Energy Projects: Encourage small-scale renewable energy projects, such as building solar cookers or wind turbines, to demonstrate sustainable practices. c. o Engaging in mitigation measures is essential at individual and community levels o Engaging in mitigation measures means actively taking steps to reduce or prevent the release of greenhouse gases (GHGs) that contribute to climate change. o Engaging in mitigation means making conscious choices at individual, community, levels to create a low-carbon and sustainable future. o The goal of mitigation is to slow down global warming and minimize its harmful effects on the environment, human health, and economies. Levels of engagement may be as follows; Individual Level  Energy Efficiency & Renewable Energy  Use energy-efficient appliances (LED bulbs, Energy Star-rated devices).  Reduce electricity use by turning off unused lights and electronics.  Install solar panels or opt for renewable energy sources if available.  Sustainable Transportation  Use public transport, biking, or walking instead of driving.  Carpool or drive fuel-efficient, hybrid, or electric vehicles (EVs).  Support policies that invest in clean public transportation.  Waste Reduction & Sustainable Consumption  Reduce, reuse, and recycle to minimize landfill waste.  Compost organic waste to lower methane emissions.  Choose sustainable, low-carbon footprint products and reduce plastic use.  Food & Agriculture Choices  Eat more plant-based meals and reduce food waste.  Support local and organic farming to reduce emissions from food transportation.  Grow home gardens or participate in community gardens. Community level  Participate in tree planting programs (trees absorb CO₂).  Advocate for bike lanes, green spaces, and energy-efficient buildings.  Support or join local sustainability projects and climate action groups. c. o Sharing information on climate change with family and community members means educating and informing those around you about the causes, effects, and potential solutions to climate change. o It involves explaining the science behind global warming, its impact on the environment, economy, and society, and the importance of collective action to address the crisis. o This can include discussing topics like carbon emissions, renewable energy, sustainable practices, and how individuals can reduce their carbon footprints. o The goal is to raise awareness, inspire action, and encourage positive environmental behaviors within your community. o It’s also about fostering a sense of responsibility and urgency, helping others understand how climate change may personally affect them and what steps can be taken at the local level to make a difference. c.  Build climate-resilient buildings, on higher ground away from river banks with improved drainage systems,  Develop early warning systems: Listen to weather forecasts and be aware of flood prone areas  Emergence preparedness; Keep emergence supplies such as food, clean water and first aid kit ready  Water Conservation: During the dry season, water can be scarce. f. Summary
Weather and Climate
 Weather: In Zambia, weather changes from day to day. For example, during the rainy
season (November to April), you might experience heavy rains and thunderstorms,
while the dry season (May to October) is characterized by clear skies and cooler
temperatures, especially in the mornings and evenings.
 Climate: Zambia has a tropical climate with three distinct seasons: Rainy Season
(November to April): Warm and wet, with most of the country's annual rainfall
occurring during this period. Cool Dry Season (May to August): Mild temperatures and
dry conditions. Hot Dry Season (September to October): High temperatures and very
dry conditions.
Climate Change
 In Zambia, climate change is observed through increasing temperatures, changing
rainfall patterns, and more frequent extreme weather events such as droughts and
floods.
 Causes: Activities like deforestation for agriculture, charcoal production, and the
burning of fossil fuels contribute to greenhouse gas emissions.
 Effects: Climate change impacts agriculture, water resources, and health. For example,
prolonged droughts can lead to reduced crop yields and water shortages, affecting food
security and access to clean water. Increased temperatures and changes in precipitation
patterns can also influence the spread of diseases like malaria.
Mitigation: Zambia is taking steps to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions and mitigate the
effects of climate change by engaging in initiatives such as tree planting and caring, use of
sustainable mobility, waste disposal in waste receptacles and waste cycling.
Adaptation: Zambia is also implementing strategies to adapt to the changing climate such as
, building climate resilient houses, promoting drought resistant crops, coping with extreme heat
and overall disaster preparedness
